title: Convex Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Optimization, I
contribution: Summer-school slides (with Linderoth) presenting convex-MINLP methods (NLP-BB, OA, Benders, ECP, LP/NLP-BB) as choices within one component grid: relaxation, constraint enforcement, upper bounds.
problem_entry: Convex MINLP under assumptions A1-A3 (bounded polyhedral X, convex C2 functions, a CQ); multi-tree methods motivated by MILP software maturity and no CQs for MILP, single-tree by missing MILP warm starts (pp. 3, 27, 41).
key_idea: Every MINLP solver = relaxation + constraint enforcement (refinement, branching, spatial branching) + upper bounds; methods placed in that grid (pp. 5, 9, 34, 43).
assumptions: B&B 'It Works Theorem' assumes bounded polyhedral X and an NLP solver returning the global min; OA convergence under A1-A3; A3 stated as stronger than needed (pp. 3, 19, 38).
proof_devices: OA finite convergence sketch: NLP optimality gives eta >= f(j), convexity gives supporting hyperplanes (p. 38)
Benders cut derived by summing OA cuts with NLP multipliers and eliminating x_C via KKT, hence Benders weaker than OA (pp. 39-40)
positioning: Credits Duran-Grossmann, Geoffrion, Westerlund-Pettersson, Bonami et al.; places own FilMINT beside BONMIN (pp. 27, 43, 50).
writing: Slide bullets with ellipsis-style motivation lines ('... motivates single-tree methods next ...'); draft marker 'Exercise ... add ECP???' left in (pp. 39, 41).
limits_future: Worst-case OA example also applies to Benders and ECP; no MILP warm starts in multi-tree methods; ECP not covered (p. 41).

method_links.note: Component decomposition (relaxation, constraint enforcement, upper bounds) as building blocks; LP/NLP-BB interleaves NLP solves inside the MILP tree
MILP preferred because it needs no constraint qualifications

title: Joint ptycho-tomography reconstruction through alternating direction method of multipliers
contribution: ADMM consensus formulation that couples ptychographic phase retrieval and tomography through a dual variable, with KKT-derived stopping tests, relaxing probe-overlap requirements on synthetic data.
problem_entry: Two-step 3D ptychography imposes rigid acquisition constraints (lateral probe overlap); prior joint method alternates single steps without connecting the subproblems (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Consensus constraints psi_theta = h_theta(x) plus ADMM: phase retrieval gets a proximal term toward the tomographic estimate, the dual update connects the two steps; few gradient steps per subproblem (pp. 3-4, 8).
assumptions: Known probe; phase in [0, 2pi) without unwrapping; Lemma 2.1 needs full column rank and exact solves, admitted void for inexact solves (pp. 6-7).
proof_devices: Stopping test from KKT conditions of the consensus problem, with extra residuals for inexact subproblems (pp. 4-5)
Lemma 2.1 equivalence of log-linearized and original tomography step by comparing first-order conditions (p. 7)
experiments: Synthetic 64^3 phantom, 30%/70% overlap, 100/400 angles, Poisson noise; inner/outer iteration sweep (Table 1); sequential and coupled baselines at equal iterations 'for a fair comparison' (pp. 8-11).
positioning: Extends Gursoy's alternating coupling [2]; ADMM credited to Glowinski-Marroco, Gabay-Mercier, Boyd et al. (pp. 2, 5).
writing: Hedged on theory: convergence 'observed', proof left to a forthcoming paper; conclusions claim robustness and acquisition flexibility (pp. 7, 14).
limits_future: No convergence proof for inexact solves; computational performance not addressed; probe retrieval, log-polar tomography and TomoPy release as future work (pp. 7, 13).

title: Optimization-based simultaneous alignment and reconstruction in multi-element tomography
contribution: Joint multi-channel Poisson-likelihood inversion that recovers projection drifts and elemental concentrations together in XRF tomography, shown on one real dataset to be more robust to low SNR than alternating and per-channel alignment.
problem_entry: Nanoscale XRF tomography is vulnerable to drift; pre-alignment and alternating reprojection fall short for significant drift; single-channel alignment fails at poor SNR (p. 2).
key_idea: Gaussian-smoothed shift operator makes drifts differentiable; channels combined with SNR-proportional weights in one objective; truncated Newton with projected CG (p. 3).
assumptions: Same error in all channels; CoR at detector center; horizontal drift only; 2D slice (pp. 2-3).
experiments: One real cell dataset (48 projections over 141 deg, six elements); baselines manual hotspot and TomoPy v1.2.1 alternating; channel ablations; median of automated methods as reference; SNR reduced to 30%-3% (pp. 3-5).
positioning: Builds on Austin-Di-Leyffer-Wild [24]; critiques manual and alternating practice by comparison, not attack (pp. 2-4).
writing: Letter format; claims 'robust and automatic' with figure-based evidence; closing sentence on vital role of such approaches (p. 5).
limits_future: 3D extension 'natural'; faster processing by in-plane parallelization (p. 5).

title: Simultaneous sensing error recovery and tomographic inversion using an optimization-based approach
contribution: Models center-of-rotation drift as a differentiable translation of the measured sinogram and recovers it jointly with the image (explicit and implicit formulations, truncated Newton), outperforming oracle-tuned regularization and TomoPy's alternating alignment on synthetic data (read as arXiv v2).
problem_entry: Small CoR drift causes large reconstruction errors; regularization, mirrored-pair, cross-correlation and iterative reprojection are insufficient or not fully coupled (arXiv pp. 1-3).
key_idea: P_theta = x*(1 - cos theta) + y* sin theta turns CoR drift into a data-side translation, done by Gaussian-regularized delta convolution via DFT, so the projection matrix is built once; explicit (CoR) vs implicit (shift) formulations (arXiv pp. 4-9).
assumptions: C2 object for the error bound; W >= 0 as the only regularizer; 2D; solutions non-unique up to translation/rotation (arXiv pp. 6, 9, 11).
proof_devices: Error O(sigma^2) + O(1/(sigma N_tau)) split into regularization, truncation and discretization terms (arXiv pp. 6, 22)
Trapezoid error bounded via a bounded-variation result (Proposition C.1, arXiv p. 23)
Flop count per truncated-Newton iteration (arXiv p. 10)
experiments: Synthetic Shepp-Logan and MRI, N = 128, 30 angles; SSIM metric; baselines no recovery, L2/TV with SSIM-optimal lambda, mirror alignment, TomoPy 1.1.3 alternating under 4%-22% noise; five CoR initializations (arXiv pp. 10-19).
positioning: Positions against Bayesian/regularization, mirror alignment, cross-correlation and iterative reprojection; critique by stated deficiency (incomplete coupling) (arXiv pp. 2-3).
writing: Opens with a striking one-figure failure example (2% CoR shift); explicit outline paragraph; conclusions recommend the implicit approach for noisy data (arXiv pp. 2-3, 19).
limits_future: Computational complexity; parallel or multigrid acceleration; priors on CoR dynamics; no real data (arXiv p. 19).

method_links.note: Competing regularizer given an oracle-best lambda, called impractical, and still beaten; competitor version stated (TomoPy 1.1.3)

title: A Lagrangian dual approach for identifying the worst contingencies in power systems
contribution: Single-level Lagrangian-dual reformulation of the AC worst-contingency bilevel problem (bound as tight as SDP) solved by a single-tree extended cutting-plane method with finite global convergence, plus a structured line-flow relaxation that scales past mixed-integer SOC.
problem_entry: Max-min line attack with nonconvex ACOPF lower level; DC models too crude, KKT reformulations violate CQs everywhere, SOC less accurate than SDP (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Dualize the lower level to get a concave mixed-binary problem with one eigenvalue constraint eta(pi) >= 0, cut lazily within one CPLEX tree (1T-ECP); structured relaxation drops 2|L| dimensions (pp. 7, 11-12, 15, 18).
assumptions: Feasible, bounded affine region; g_N convex nonsmooth locally Lipschitz; duality under mild CQs; line flow bounds relaxed (pp. 12, 14, 15, 19).
proof_devices: Proposition 1: inner infimum as minimum-eigenvalue indicator (p. 7)
Lemma 1: finite inner loop by contradiction with an accumulation point, Lipschitz ball of radius min{eps/(3L), delta} and an earlier cut (p. 14)
Theorem 1: finite global termination from finitely many nodes plus Lemma 1 (p. 14)
Proposition 5 chain of bounds Phi_SOC <= Phi_SDP = Phi_AC_D <= Phi_AC (p. 11)
experiments: IEEE 30-300 and Pegase 1354/2869 buses, K = 1-4, 24 h, single core; self-built miSDP B&B and Mosek miSOC baselines; losses and memory failures reported (pp. 15-19).
positioning: Improves on the SOC approach of Wu et al. [WCA18]; single-tree idea credited to Quesada-Grossmann [QG92] (pp. 2, 11).
writing: Four numbered contributions in the introduction; preprint still has unresolved 'Tables ??' references (pp. 2, 16).
limits_future: Exponentially many dense cuts and master-update time; future cut aggregation, spectral bundle/proximal methods, hybrid with mixed-integer SDP branching (pp. 19-20).

method_links.note: KKT reformulation rejected because it violates CQs at every feasible point; linear master chosen so MILP presolve helps

title: Compact Representations of BFGS Matrices
contribution: Compact representations of the two structured BFGS updates of Petra et al., enabling limited-memory structured BFGS line-search methods with SMW search directions and four initializations, tested on CUTEst, LIBSVM, PDE control and against IPOPT and L-BFGS.
problem_entry: Structured objectives with known and unknown Hessian parts; S-BFGS-M/P updates lack a compact form, hence no limited-memory version (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: Derive compact factored forms (Theorems 2.1, 2.3) and build L-S-BFGS-M/P line-search algorithms with SMW solves (pp. 5-12).
assumptions: f twice continuously differentiable; s_k^T u_k > 0 for positive definiteness; efficient solves with K_k for large n (pp. 3-4, 12).
proof_devices: Shift by K_{k+1} reduces S-BFGS-M to standard BFGS in u_k, inheriting the Byrd-Nocedal-Schnabel compact form (pp. 4-5)
experiments: Synthetic quadratics for initialization tuning; CUTEst set of [18] (61 vs 62 problems stated); 10 LIBSVM problems; PDE control up to n = 9604; IPOPT 3.12.12 and L-BFGS on a structured quartic; extended performance profiles (pp. 14-24).
positioning: Extends Byrd et al. compact representation and Petra et al. structured updates; earlier structured QN for least squares credited (pp. 3-4).
writing: Short contributions subsection; conclusions phrased as rules of thumb per variant (pp. 5, 24).
limits_future: No convergence analysis and no future-work paragraph; recommendations limited to initialization choices (p. 24).

title: MPEC methods for bilevel optimization problems
contribution: Survey of MPEC reformulations of optimistic bilevel problems: stationarity concepts and MPEC CQs, NLP-based and combinatorial algorithms with their convergence guarantees, and modelling/solver software.
problem_entry: Optimistic bilevel with convex lower level satisfying a CQ, replaced by lower-level KKT to give an MPEC; moral-hazard example (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Classify MPEC methods by what stationarity they guarantee: NLP methods (relaxation, penalty, elastic, AL) mostly C-stationary, combinatorial (pivoting, B&B, SLPEC-EQP) reach B-stationarity (pp. 10-16).
assumptions: C1 functions; bilevel-MPEC equivalence for global solutions under Slater, not for local ones; Fritz-John variant discouraged computationally (pp. 2-3).
proof_devices: Tangent-cone decomposition over NLP pieces (eqs. (8)-(9), p. 6)
Quadratic local SQP convergence for the slack reformulation with a counterexample showing slacks are needed (p. 11)
SQPEC counterexample with closed-form iterates converging to an M-stationary point (p. 15)
positioning: Consolidates own MPEC line (FilterMPEC, MPECs as NLPs, SQP local convergence, SLPEC filter, MacMPEC) next to Scholtes, Kanzow-Schwartz, Anitescu, DeMiguel et al. (pp. 10-17).
writing: Remark 1 states the practical verdict (NLP methods most practical, but may stop at C-stationary points); claims of uniqueness hedged 'to our knowledge' (pp. 14, 16).
limits_future: No robust large-scale bilevel solver exists; pessimistic, nonconvex lower level, SOCP, stochastic, discrete, multiobjective extensions not covered (pp. 17-18).

title: Pufferscale: Rescaling HPC data services for high energy physics applications
contribution: Formalizes rescaling of microservice-based HPC storage as a three-objective placement problem, justifies the objectives with exact small-instance MIP solves, and gives a weighted greedy heuristic implemented in Pufferscale and evaluated at up to 2,048 emulated servers.
problem_entry: HEPnOS cannot be rescaled; classical load rebalancing ignores data balance and slows later decommissions (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Minimize max load, max data and transfer duration (eqs. (1)-(7)); exact CPLEX solves show all three matter; greedy LPT-style heuristic with user weights (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Homogeneous cluster, network bottleneck, no replication, in-memory storage; normally distributed bucket sizes and loads (pp. 3-4, 7).
experiments: Exact solves 1 h 40 min on average for 8 servers/32 buckets; heuristic emulated up to 2,048 servers and 8,192 buckets on Grid'5000, 100 repetitions, lower bounds as reference since no fair competitor fits; heuristic <= 612 ms (pp. 4, 7).
positioning: Distinguishes from single-criterion rebalancing (Rao et al., Ceph, HDFS) and VM rebalancing (pp. 2-3).
writing: Numbered contribution list mapped to sections; evaluation scope limited explicitly by 'space constraints' (pp. 2, 7).
limits_future: Application speedup not evaluated; replication open; DFO (POUNDERS) tuning of weights suggested (pp. 7, 9-10).

method_links.note: No fair external baseline; lower bounds replace competitors and the reason is stated
